column3: Near-verbatim parallel: every kind of example is set forth for people in this Qur'an.
Its deliberate mixing and concealment of truth clarifies the falsehood charge that blocks reception of the focus's signs.
Contrasts following falsehood with following truth and explicitly frames examples for people.
Near-verbatim parallel: varied examples in the Qur'an are met by widespread refusal and disbelief.
The immediate continuation explains the repeated rejection as hearts sealed against knowing.
Its call for upright speech offers only a broad contrast to the false accusation in the focus.
Closely repeats the Qur'anic setting forth of every example and adds the human tendency to dispute.
The nearby correction of those who did not know supports the focus's diagnosis of resistant hearers.
Names the Qur'an as clear, a broad background to its evidentiary role in the focus.
Shows disbelievers refusing this Qur'an outright, matching the focus's hostile response to revelation.
The term for representational forms is only a lexical echo and does not develop the focus's evidentiary theme.
Explicitly identifies disbelievers as those who reject God's signs after the Book is sent down.
States that examples were given to every people before their destruction, extending the focus's warning function.
The immediate sequel tells the messenger to endure those without certainty after their rejection.
Directly links disbelief to rejecting God's signs, the response anticipated in the focus.
Its denial of the Hour after receiving mercy is a related but less direct pattern of unbelief.
The nearby scene shows criminals making a false claim at the Hour, reinforcing the local pattern of distortion.
Describes a Book brought and detailed with knowledge, guidance, and mercy, supporting the sufficiency of revealed evidence.
Those told of resurrection call it manifest magic, closely paralleling dismissal of a sign rather than engagement with it.
It exposes a fabricated spoken claim, but not specifically a response to Qur'anic examples or signs.
Rejects a more guided message without testing it, exemplifying the fixed filter described in the focus.
Signs meant as warning increase great transgression, showing evidence can be met with intensified resistance.
As the surah opening, it supplies only distant local context for the focus.
Moses' plain declaration of messengerhood is a general precedent for presenting a divine claim.
Shows opportunistic speech under pressure, a broad contrast to a settled response to truth.
Its universal submission theme has only a distant relation to the focus's human refusal.
Attributes denial to the transgressing sinner, identifying a moral disposition behind rejection.
Says messengers bring signs only by God's permission and that false-makers lose when His command comes.
Explicitly identifies these as examples set forth for people and ties their comprehension to knowledge.
Rejects inherited wrongdoing as an excuse, but does not directly concern signs or examples.
Treats mockery of God, His signs, and His messenger as a culpable response to revelation.
The opening prediction is remote local context rather than a direct parallel to the focus's reception scene.
Directly counters the claim of human fabrication, the source-directed rejection named in the focus.
The call to gather a crowd has no substantive connection to examples, signs, or their rejection.
The immediately preceding judgment scene shows that wrongdoers' excuses will no longer avail them.
Disbelievers describe the summoned Day as difficult, a later expression of resistance rather than a response to proof.
Despite manifest signs given through Jesus, disbelievers label them manifest magic.
The broken idols may provoke reflection, but the passage does not directly address the focus's sign-response pattern.
It names despair as unbelief, a broad but indirect description of a rejecting stance.
Affirms that a messenger brings a sign only by God's permission, framing the status of the focus's sign.
The predicted reversal is only distant local context for the focus.
The community's accusation over an unexpected event loosely parallels hostile reception of evidence.
Records demands for a sign and answers them by the messenger's adherence to revealed insight, guidance, and mercy.
Sectarian satisfaction with partial holdings is a broad model of closed reception, not a direct sign parallel.
The hearers answer an extraordinary claim by calling it an enormous offense, resembling dismissal by accusation.
Pharaoh demands that Moses produce his sign if he is truthful, directly staging a contested evidentiary claim.
Its truth-falsehood contrast supports the focus's opposition between divine evidence and the charge of falsehood.
Even recitation to the audience does not produce belief, matching the focus's persistence of refusal.
Acknowledging God as Creator while maintaining powerless alternatives is an indirect example of inconsistent response.
The local assertion of God's unfailing promise and widespread ignorance supports the surrounding argument.
Forbids inventing examples for God, providing a focused contrast to God's own setting forth of examples.
Rescue followed by association partners is a related pattern of failing to respond rightly to clear evidence.
The nearby verse recalls messengers bringing clear proofs, followed by judgment on criminals and help for believers.
Explicitly calls the event a sign while observing that most still do not believe.
Uses a divinely given example to make the transience of worldly life intelligible.
A clear surviving sign is left for people who understand, extending the focus's evidence-and-response theme.
Connects the lasting Fire directly to persistent rejection of God's signs.
Its legal comparison of compensation is unrelated to the focus's examples or rejection of signs.
The nearby assertion of creation and return undergirds the surah's evidentiary argument.
The warning against slanderers has no material link to the focus's examples or signs.
God sets forth examples distinguishing enduring truth from vanishing falsehood, directly illuminating the focus's falsehood charge.
The nearby response to a blighting wind shows people persisting in disbelief despite another sign.
Its degraded worship and consequent punishment relate broadly to disbelief but not to the focus's proof pattern.
Moses and Aaron explicitly announce that they have come with a sign from the Lord.
It brands an attributed claim as a lie, but offers no direct treatment of signs or Qur'anic examples.
A parable of worldly life is followed by the statement that signs are detailed for reflective people.
The travel verb is only a lexical match and the passage concerns testamentary witnesses.
The local call to glorify God supplies context but not a direct link to rejection of signs.
The boastful speaker illustrates arrogance, a possible disposition behind rejection but not a direct parallel.
The arrival of truth exposes and removes falsehood, directly answering the focus's accusation of falsity.
The nearby verse identifies desire without knowledge as the basis for wrongful following.
God's teaching of the Qur'an supports the focus's presentation of it as the medium of examples.
Proclaims the arrival of truth and the impotence of falsehood, echoing the focus's contested truth claim.
Part of a false attribution, it is only indirectly related to the focus's accusation of falsehood.
Directly denies that the Qur'an can be forged and describes it as confirming and detailing the Book.
Repeated exposition in the Qur'an is met with increased aversion, closely matching the focus's resistant audience.
The local praise of God supplies only general surah context.
Its parable contrasts those unable to receive with those who see and hear, modeling divergent responses to evidence.
Explicitly says such examples are set forth for people so that they may reflect on the Qur'an.
A creation sign for listeners is relevant only at the broad level of signs in the same surah.
The companion rebukes disbelief through creation, a broad precedent for confronting denial with evidence.
Even a tangible Book handled by hand would be called manifest magic, closely paralleling the focus's invariant rejection.
Past destruction is presented as a recurring consequence for disbelievers, extending the warning force of the focus's examples.
It explicitly names disbelief in God's signs as the cause of loss.
People see the fate of prior wrongdoers and receive examples, making examples concrete warnings rather than mere illustration.
A nearby creation sign and call to gratitude is only a broad contextual parallel.
The travelers' fatigue and request for food do not connect to the focus's evidentiary theme.
The inheritance allocation passage has no substantive relation to examples, signs, or their rejection.
The nearby life-from-death argument concludes with human resurrection, supplying evidence in the same discourse.
Disbelievers rushing toward the messenger shows hostile attention, but not the focus's specific response to proof.
Listeners privately characterize the messenger as bewitched, a direct instance of displacing evidence with an attack on its bearer.
Even every sign would not change their response before painful punishment, directly confirming that the issue is not lack of evidence.
The Book given to Moses for guidance is a general precedent for revelation's guiding purpose.
It explicitly identifies a sign while noting that most people still do not believe.
The messenger's role and God's witness offer only a broad background to the focus's address to people.
Its universal divine power and knowledge do not directly develop the focus's examples or rejection.
The failure to understand speech is a broad analogue to the focus's closed reception.
The oath by the wise Qur'an supports the authority of the Qur'an in which the focus says examples are set forth.
Its command to call steadfastly despite others' desires broadly supports persistence amid refusal.
Universal future gathering is only a distant eschatological background to the focus.
God sets forth even a small example, while the same evidence guides believers and increases others in defiance.
Clear signs are sent down, yet only the defiantly disobedient disbelieve in them.
Those without knowledge demand that God speak directly or bring a sign, repeating an entrenched evidentiary demand.
Every sign from their Lord is met by turning away, directly expressing the focus's invariant rejection.
They deny the truth when it comes to them, supplying the broader pattern behind the focus's falsehood accusation.
A demand for an angelic sign shows that proposed proof is continually displaced by a new requirement.
Veiled hearts and deafness leave hearers calling the Qur'an ancient tales, combining non-reception with dismissal.
It distinguishes calling the messenger a liar from actually rejecting God's signs, directly matching the focus's source-directed accusation.
The messenger is confronted with their aversion even when he is urged to bring them a sign.
Their demand for a sign is answered by God's ability to send one and by their lack of knowledge.
Those who deny God's signs are reached by punishment because of their defiant departure.
Even an oath-backed sign is not assumed to produce belief, exposing that the obstacle is not merely proof quantity.
Even angels, direct speech, and gathered signs would not make them believe unless God willed.
They refuse to believe until granted a messenger-like sign themselves, turning revelation into a status demand.
Those who deny the signs and act arrogantly toward them receive a definitive consequence.
The arrogant are turned from the signs; even seeing every sign, they do not believe and choose the path of error.
Denying God's signs and the meeting to come renders prior works void.
When the verses are recited, they are dismissed as tales of earlier peoples.
Those who reject the encounter with God ask for another Qur'an or for this one to be changed.
They demand a sign from the messenger's Lord despite the Qur'anic warning already before them.
When truth reaches them, they label it manifest magic rather than examine its claim.
Disbelievers again demand a sign from the messenger, while his role is framed as warning.
The recurring demand for a sign is answered by God's governance of guidance rather than by an evidentiary concession.
It portrays a hypothetical Qur'an of overwhelming effects, yet continues the question of whether rejection would cease.
The recipient of the Reminder is called mad, directly exemplifying an attack on the bearer instead of the message.
Even an opened gate in heaven would be reclassified as dazzled sight or magic.
When one sign is replaced with another, opponents call the messenger an inventor of falsehood.
The claim that a human teaches the messenger directly shifts the issue from the message to an alleged human source.
Those who do not believe in God's signs are described as refusing the route of guidance.
It identifies fabricators of lies with those who do not believe in God's signs.
A hidden barrier is placed between the Qur'an and those who deny the Hereafter.
Covered hearts and deaf ears make hearers turn away when God alone is mentioned in the Qur'an.
Earlier peoples' denial of signs explains why requested signs are not simply sent on demand.
The hearers demand spectacular material proofs as conditions for belief.
Their escalating demands show the continuing relocation of the burden of proof.
The refusal to believe when guidance comes is attributed to resistance to a human messenger.
Nothing prevents belief and forgiveness except waiting for the fate of earlier deniers or for punishment to arrive.
Pharaoh calls Moses' sign magic and recasts its purpose as an attempt to expel his people.
They demand a sign from the messenger despite prior clear proofs in earlier scriptures.
The revelation is alternately called confused dreams, fabricated poetry, and then answered with a demand for a sign.
When clear verses are recited, hostility appears on the faces of disbelievers and approaches violence against reciters.
They call the Qur'an a fabricated falsehood aided by others, directly mirroring the focus's charge.
They dismiss it as ancient tales written down and dictated to the messenger.
Clear, visible signs are called manifest magic after they come to the people.
They reject the signs despite inward certainty, out of wrongdoing and arrogance.
When Moses brings clear signs, they are labeled fabricated magic and denied any such precedent.
When truth comes, it is called magic; previous signs are also dismissed as two supporting magical displays.
The Qur'an is described as clear signs, while only wrongdoers reject God's signs.
The demand for further signs is answered by locating signs with God and the messenger's task in clear warning.
The recited Book is explicitly presented as sufficient despite the demand for other signs.
The evil end of wrongdoers follows their denial and mockery of God's signs.
The immediate sequel states that the messenger cannot make the dead hear, explaining the limits of further address to refusal.
The immediate sequel adds that the blind cannot be guided from error and only those who submit can be made to hear.
When God's verses are recited, the hearer turns away arrogantly as though he had not heard them.
No one is more unjust than one reminded by God's signs who then turns away from them.
Clear verses are met by calling the messenger a would-be diversion and the Qur'an a fabricated lie.
The prior word has come true for most of them, so they do not believe.
Successive messengers are met with mockery, extending the rejection pattern beyond a single sign.
The arrival of a warner is answered by calling him a magician and a liar.
Only disbelievers dispute concerning God's signs; their activity must not mislead the messenger.
Disbelievers urge one another not to listen to the Qur'an and to drown it out so they may prevail.
When truth comes, it is called magic and explicitly rejected.
They turn away from a clear messenger and call him one taught by others or mad.
God's verses are recited in truth, yet the question is posed what message they will believe after God and His signs.
A hearer of God's verses persists arrogantly as though he had not heard them.
When clear verses are recited, the truth that arrives is dismissed as manifest magic.
On seeing a sign, they turn away and call it continuing magic.
The revelatory message is reduced to magic handed down from earlier times.
